Why Does This Report Matter?

Ports play a critical role in international trade, regional and domestic economic activities, and the
well-being of people and societies. Today, ports are no longer simply physical infrastructure; they
have become digital systems. Port authorities, terminal operators, shipping lines, logistics providers,
and customs are increasingly linked through shared digital platforms. This improves efficiency and
transparency in ports, but it also means that a breach in one part of the ecosystem can cascade
across others. Cybersecurity in ports is therefore a collective responsibility, and the entire ecosystem
is only as strong as its weakest link.

A cybersecurity incident at a port can halt vessel movements, prevent cargo from reaching its
destination, and compromise the safety of people and the integrity of equipment, such as robot
cranes or guided vehicles. The costs of incidents

respondents from ports in high-income countries than among ports in low- and middle-income

lower-middle-income (57 percent) contexts, this share is much lower. It drops to 38 percent among
respondents from ports in low-income countries. This is likely due to the higher maturity levels of the
legal requirements in high-income countries, as illustrated by the examples listed in Table 1 in the
